why_angle: The only answer the shopper got gives size bands and a generic calculator but never checks a real kit: it doesn't show that the maker's 14.4 kWh/day for the SGR-8K10E is panel watts times sun hours with no losses (about 10.8 kWh after 25% losses), that its 10.24 kWh battery holds under one day of that, or how the panel strings compare with the inverter's 500 V limit. This page gives those figures for every kit, each worked from maker data opened 2026-11-13.

page.title: DIY Off-Grid Solar System Kits Sized by Daily kWh
page.h1: DIY off grid solar system: four one-cart kits, sized by daily kWh
page.desc: Four one-cart DIY off-grid solar system kits compared by daily kWh after losses, days of battery, 120/240 V output and panel string voltage against the 500 V limit.
page.answer: Short answer. For most DIY off grid solar systems, the Sun Gold Power SGR-8K10E kit fits: its 3,600 W of panels make about 10.8 kWh a day at 4 peak sun hours after 25% losses. Pick the kit whose daily kWh covers your use; its 10.24 kWh battery holds just under one day of that.

page.after:
What the differences mean

Every kit is worked out the same way: panel watts × 4 peak sun hours × 0.75. The 0.75 is Dealectric's planning allowance for wiring, heat, inverter and battery losses. Sun Gold Power's own figure of 14.4 kWh a day for the SGR-8K10E is 3,600 W × 4 h with nothing taken off. Days of battery means storage ÷ daily solar. If you keep 20% of the battery in reserve, multiply it by 0.8. Prices are the store's on 2026-11-13.

  • SGR-8K10E: 3,600 W × 4 h × 0.75 = 10.8 kWh/day. 10.24 kWh ÷ 10.8 = 0.95 day. $4,949 ÷ 10.8 = $458 per daily kWh.
  • SGR-8K10E + 1 SG48100P: still 10.8 kWh/day. 15.36 kWh ÷ 10.8 = 1.42 days. $4,949 + $981 = $5,930, or $549 per daily kWh.
  • SGR-10K20E: 5,400 W × 4 h × 0.75 = 16.2 kWh/day. 20.48 kWh ÷ 16.2 = 1.26 days. $8,390 ÷ 16.2 = $518 per daily kWh.
  • SGM-5K5E: 1,200 W × 4 h × 0.75 = 3.6 kWh/day. 5.12 kWh ÷ 3.6 = 1.42 days. $2,831 ÷ 3.6 = $786 per daily kWh.

{kit:kit-8kw-10kwh-cabin} The SGR-8K10E suits most builds. It has 120/240 V split-phase output and two built-in MPPT inputs rated for up to 11,000 W of panels. Its batteries talk to the inverter over RS485. The kit includes a 200 A DC breaker, a 25 A PV breaker, 2/0 AWG cables, a 250 A busbar and Z-brackets. Bought separately, the 8 kW inverter ($1,305) and a 2-pack of SG48100P ($1,953) come to $3,258. That leaves $1,691 of the kit price, about $211 a panel, to cover the eight panels plus all the breakers, cables and brackets.

{kit:kit-8kw-15kwh-extra-battery} If your use stays near 10 kWh a day but you want a cloudy day covered, add one more SG48100P ($981) to the same cart. It is the battery the kit already ships with. It speaks CAN/RS485/RS232 and runs up to 63 in parallel. That takes storage from 0.95 to 1.42 days for $2,460 less than the 10 kW kit.

{kit:kit-10kw-20kwh-full-time} Choose the SGR-10K20E when you use more than about 11 kWh a day. Its 5.4 kW of panels yield 16.2 kWh a day after losses, which neither 8 kW kit can match without more panels.

{kit:kit-5kw-small-cabin-120v} The SGM-5K5E is the lowest buy-in at $2,831. It outputs 120 V only, though, and has the highest cost per daily kWh of the four, so buy it only for small, 120 V-only loads.

Size by daily kWh, then check the panel strings

The inverter's watts set how much can run at once. The daily kWh decides whether the battery is full again by evening. That is why the table leads with daily solar after losses rather than inverter size. For the SGR-8K10E, the 3,600 W of panels use only 33% of the inverter's 11,000 W PV rating (3,600 ÷ 11,000), so you can add panels later without changing the inverter.

Wiring is the next thing to check. The 8 kW inverter's manual says the open-circuit voltage of panels in series must stay below 500 V. The store lists both the 8 kW and 10 kW inverters at 500 V DC open-circuit, the 10 kW at each of its two inputs. The table below uses the SGN-450-BDG5 450 W panel's figures: Voc 35.03 V, Vmp 30.08 V, Isc 16.05 A.

LayoutOpen-circuit voltageWorking voltage (Vmp)Current into one input
8 in series (SGR-8K10E)8 × 35.03 = 280.2 V8 × 30.08 = 240.6 V16.05 A
2 strings of 4 on one input4 × 35.03 = 140.1 V4 × 30.08 = 120.3 V2 × 16.05 = 32.1 A
12 in series (SGR-10K20E)12 × 35.03 = 420.4 V12 × 30.08 = 361.0 V16.05 A
2 strings of 6, one per input6 × 35.03 = 210.2 V6 × 30.08 = 180.5 V16.05 A each

One string of 8 leaves 219.8 V below the 500 V limit (500 − 280.2), so there is room for panel voltage to rise in cold weather. Twelve in series leaves only 79.6 V (500 − 420.4), so check the temperature coefficient on the panel label before wiring the SGR-10K20E as a single string. Two strings of 4 on one input halve the working voltage and double the current to 32.1 A. Compare both against the MPPT voltage window and per-input current limit in your inverter's manual before you use that layout. Each kit ships with one 25 A PV breaker and one 50 ft PV extension set, so using the inverter's second input means buying a second breaker and cable set.

What you still buy separately

The store's lists of what comes in these kits include Z-brackets, a DC breaker, a PV breaker and battery cables. They name no roof or ground racking, grounding hardware, AC disconnect or load center. Budget for those on top of the kit price. Plan for the panel wiring to the inverter and the AC side to be inspected under your local electrical code.
